messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The collapse of her younger brother’s breathing in the emergency department left Aroha with a mind that could not unlearn the geometry of that room. She remembered the exact contour of the ICU waiting area, the way the narrow corridors forced her into a confined aisle, and the relentless antiseptic sting that clung to her coat long after they wheeled him away. When the staff began speaking in overlapping, technical cadences that dissolved into incomprehensible chatter, she felt the floor tilt beneath her. Those three sensations—the confining physical space, the sterile chemical scent, the garbled vocal rush—became her first warning system. Whenever Aroha now walked past a clinic entrance or caught that same chemical tang in a newly finished architectural model, her pulse spiked, and the old terror that she would lose him all over again rushed back. Those unavoidable spatial cues and chemical odors did more than spark panic; they fundamentally altered how she viewed herself. She was certain that her vulnerability was stamped across her face, that others could see exactly what had happened to her. She had come to believe the world was hostile, that her faith in people and any higher power had evaporated, leaving her with a hollow conviction that nothing she designed or achieved could ever hold meaning again. Aroha’s responses solidified over the following months. The moment she recognized those spatial boundaries or caught the hospital smell drifting from a colleague’s hand sanitizer at her firm, she immediately retreated. She stopped answering phone calls, telling friends she was overwhelmed when she was actually locking her studio door. She began pushing herself through grueling, solitary runs until her muscles trembled, and she avoided all medical cues, swerving her car at ambulance sirens and cancelling every routine physical exam. These compulsive workouts and social withdrawals offered temporary relief, yet they quickly bred the very fears they were meant to silence. Isolating from her friends and exhausting her body convinced her that she was fundamentally broken and utterly alone, which only deepened her conviction that she was exposed to others’ judgment. Pushing through endless laps and dodging social ties also kept her hyper-vigilant; her physical exhaustion lowered her threshold for stress, making every unfamiliar location and muffled conversation feel immediately threatening. Her internal landscape continued to feed the cycle. Believing she had lost all faith and that life held no meaning, Aroha stopped looking for safety and instead scanned every environment for proof of her doom. This hopeless expectation amplified her sensory alertness; when she walked into a client presentation in a glass-walled medical building, the sheer size of the open plan and the murmur of overlapping conversations triggered a panic so acute it mirrored the hospital corridor. What frightened her most was that her own avoidance had become a mirror reflecting her worst fears back at her. Because she was convinced she could not be trusted or understood, she doubled down on her withdrawal. She interpreted her own anxiety as a personal failing, which only justified her further retreat from friends and her escalation into compulsive exercise. She told herself she had no choice but to stay apart, to keep moving until the thoughts quieted, never realizing that her flight from connection and her rigid routines were the very engines keeping her terror alive. It was the day she stood paralyzed in the middle of her drafting table, unable to complete a single line for a hospital wing project, that she finally called a therapist. She had spent years drafting structures meant to shelter families, yet she could not build a single safe place for herself. She wanted the panic to stop, but she was terrified that seeking help would force her back into the very rooms, smells, and sounds that had already taught her the world was unsafe.
